ch.n: Learn › Algo Track › From Backtest to Li
ch.str: Learn › Algo Track › From Backtest to Live › Session 6 of 8

ch.n: The gap between “it worked on paper” and
ch.str: The gap between “it worked on paper” and “it is running with real money.”

ch.n: Paper Is Clean. Markets Are Not.
ch.str: Paper Is Clean. Markets Are Not.

ch.n: Part 4 showed how to test an idea on his
ch.str: Part 4 showed how to test an idea on historical data. Part 5 is about what changes when the idea starts touching the real market.

ch.n: A backtest lives in a clean world. Price
ch.str: A backtest lives in a clean world. Prices are already recorded. The data is sitting still. Orders either happen according to your assumptions or they do not. Nothing disconnects. Nothing freezes. No broker API returns a confusing error. No order gets partially filled at an awkward price.

ch.n: Live trading is different. The strategy
ch.str: Live trading is different. The strategy is no longer just a set of rules. It becomes a small operating system: reading data, making decisions, placing orders, tracking positions, enforcing limits, and knowing when to stop.

ch.n: Going live is not just “turning the back
ch.str:
Going live is not just “turning the backtest on.”

It is the moment your strategy needs execution, monitoring, and risk controls.

ch.n: What Changes When Money Is Real
ch.str: What Changes When Money Is Real

ch.n: The rules may be the same. The environme
ch.str: The rules may be the same. The environment is not.

ch.n: Historical prices are fixed. Orders are
ch.str: Historical prices are fixed. Orders are simulated. Costs are modeled. Mistakes cost nothing. You can run the same period again and again.

ch.n: Prices move while you act. Orders can mi
ch.str: Prices move while you act. Orders can miss, fill partially, or fill badly. Systems can disconnect. Mistakes cost real money and cannot be replayed.

ch.n: That does not mean live trading should f
ch.str: That does not mean live trading should feel mysterious. It means you need to name the moving parts. Once you name them, you can design around them.

ch.n: ↳ A live algo is not just strategy logic
ch.str: ↳ A live algo is not just strategy logic. It is strategy logic surrounded by operational discipline.

ch.n: You already know the basic order types.
ch.str: You already know the basic order types. In algo trading, the question becomes: which order best matches the assumptions your strategy was tested under?

ch.n: You are likely to get filled, but you gi
ch.str: You are likely to get filled, but you give up price control. In fast or illiquid markets, the fill can be worse than expected.

ch.n: You control the worst acceptable price,
ch.str: You control the worst acceptable price, but the trade may not happen if the market does not reach your limit.

ch.n: Used to trigger exits or entries when pr
ch.str: Used to trigger exits or entries when price crosses a level. Useful, but still exposed to gaps and execution quality.

ch.n: Splits execution across time. Useful whe
ch.str: Splits execution across time. Useful when a large order could move the market or attract attention.

ch.n: There is no universally “best” order typ
ch.str: There is no universally “best” order type. The right choice depends on the strategy. A fast breakout strategy may care more about getting filled. A mean-reversion strategy may care more about price discipline. The point is to make the live execution match the tested assumption as closely as possible.

ch.n: If your backtest assumes price disciplin
ch.str: If your backtest assumes price discipline, but your live system uses aggressive market orders, you are no longer trading the same strategy.

ch.n: Most live algo failures are not dramatic
ch.str: Most live algo failures are not dramatic. They are boring system problems that were not handled clearly.

ch.n: If the price feed disconnects, becomes s
ch.str: If the price feed disconnects, becomes stale, or sends bad data, the algo can make decisions on the wrong picture of the market. A live system needs to know when data is fresh, when it is stale, and when to stop acting.

ch.n: Orders can be rejected. Requests can tim
ch.str: Orders can be rejected. Requests can time out. An API can return an error after the order actually reached the broker. Your system must be able to check the real order state instead of guessing.

ch.n: You may ask to buy 10,000 shares and rec
ch.str: You may ask to buy 10,000 shares and receive only 3,000. The strategy now has a position, but not the position it expected. Live code needs to handle partial fills as a normal case, not an exception.

ch.n: A retry mechanism can accidentally submi
ch.str: A retry mechanism can accidentally submit the same order twice if it does not check whether the first order succeeded. Good systems are paranoid about duplicates because they quietly turn a normal position into an oversized one.

ch.n: ↳ This is why your first live algo shoul
ch.str: ↳ This is why your first live algo should be boring. Boring is easier to monitor, easier to debug, and easier to trust.

ch.n: A live algo needs rules that govern not
ch.str: A live algo needs rules that govern not only trades, but the system itself.

ch.n: the largest amount of capital the algo c
ch.str: the largest amount of capital the algo can put into one trade.

ch.n: the largest percentage of the account th
ch.str: the largest percentage of the account that can be deployed at once.

ch.n: the point where the system stops trading
ch.str: the point where the system stops trading for the day, even if new signals appear.

ch.n: the point where the strategy is paused a
ch.str: the point where the strategy is paused and reviewed instead of blindly continuing.

ch.n: a simple way to shut the system down imm
ch.str: a simple way to shut the system down immediately. Always.

ch.n: The risk controls must outrank the strat
ch.str:
The risk controls must outrank the strategy.

If the strategy says “buy” and the risk layer says “stop,” the answer is stop.

ch.n: When Not to Trust Your Algo
ch.str: When Not to Trust Your Algo

ch.n: A live strategy needs monitoring because
ch.str: A live strategy needs monitoring because a strategy can stop working without throwing an error.

ch.n: A strategy built on one market environme
ch.str: A strategy built on one market environment may struggle in another. Volatility changes. Interest rates change. Liquidity changes. The same rules can behave differently when the market’s personality shifts.

ch.n: Drawdown is not just something to observ
ch.str: Drawdown is not just something to observe. It is something to predefine. If the strategy falls beyond the level you said was acceptable, the system should pause. Not after a debate. Not after “one more trade.” Pause first, analyze second.

ch.n: Every strategy faces the slow possibilit
ch.str: Every strategy faces the slow possibility of decay. Once an inefficiency is widely known and traded, the edge erodes. The market does not adapt consciously, but the population of traders does. The result looks the same: your returns degrade.

ch.n: This does not mean the algo is broken in
ch.str: This does not mean the algo is broken in the technical sense. It may still run perfectly. It may still enter and exit exactly as designed. The problem is that the opportunity it used to exploit is no longer paying the same way.

ch.n: If the live strategy starts behaving ver
ch.str: If the live strategy starts behaving very differently from the backtest — more trades, longer holds, worse fills, deeper drawdowns — that difference is information. Do not ignore it because the code is still running.
↳ Monitoring rolling performance matters as much as the initial backtest. The question is not “did this strategy work once?” It is “is it still behaving like the strategy I tested?”

ch.n: Knowing When to Override Is a Skill
ch.str: Knowing When to Override Is a Skill
Automation removes emotional hesitation from execution. It does not remove human responsibility from supervision.

ch.n: A beginner mistake is thinking that once
ch.str: A beginner mistake is thinking that once a system is automated, touching it means you failed. That is not true. A live algo is not a religion. It is a tool. Tools are monitored, paused, repaired, and sometimes retired.

ch.n: The skill is not overriding because you
ch.str: The skill is not overriding because you are scared. The skill is overriding because a pre-defined condition says the system should not continue: data is stale, drawdown has breached the limit, fills are abnormal, the broker is rejecting orders, or the strategy’s live behavior no longer matches what you tested.

ch.n:
The algo does not know it is broken.

Yo
ch.str:
The algo does not know it is broken.

You design the conditions that tell it when to stop.

ch.n: The First Live Algo Should Be Boring
ch.str: The First Live Algo Should Be Boring

ch.n: Boring does not mean weak. Boring means
ch.str: Boring does not mean weak. Boring means understandable enough to supervise.

ch.n: Start with a simple strategy. Small size
ch.str: Start with a simple strategy. Small size. Clear logs. Conservative costs. No leverage. No complicated AI layer. No hidden decision logic that you cannot explain. The goal of the first live system is not to impress anyone. The goal is to learn how live execution actually behaves.

ch.n: Once you can safely run something boring
ch.str: Once you can safely run something boring, monitor it, pause it, and understand its failures, you have earned the right to make it more sophisticated.

ch.n: ↳ Good live trading is not dramatic. It
ch.str: ↳ Good live trading is not dramatic. It is controlled.

ch.n: Six things to carry into system architec
ch.str: Six things to carry into system architecture.

ch.n: ✓Going live is not just turning on a bac
ch.str: ✓Going live is not just turning on a backtest. A live algo needs execution, monitoring, and risk controls.
✓Order types matter because live execution should match the assumptions your strategy was tested under.
✓Operational problems — stale data, API errors, partial fills, duplicate orders — are normal live-system concerns.
✓Every live algo needs real-money controls: max position size, max exposure, max daily loss, drawdown thresholds, and a kill switch.
✓Strategies can stop working because of regime changes, drawdowns, alpha decay, or behavior drift.

ch.n: ✓The first live algo should be boring, s
ch.str: ✓The first live algo should be boring, small, observable, and easy to shut down.

ch.n: Architect Your Algo Like a Mini Company
ch.str:
Architect Your Algo Like a Mini Company
How serious systems are split into roles: data, research, execution, portfolio, and risk.
